sections.html:
Along PA 309 close to the Bucks County line, Montgomery Township is the biggest municipality in Montgomery County's North Penn area. The 2020 census counted 25,862 residents, and a July 2025 estimate puts the number at 26,210. Suburban neighborhoods cover most of the land. Many houses come from two building booms, the 1980s and the 1990s, when the population more than doubled and then grew another 81 percent.

Montgomery Square on PA 309 serves as the downtown, and the ZIP code is 19454. Shared villages mean some addresses fall near neighboring municipalities, so confirm the township on your tax bill before you look up any rule or rate. Colmar and Fortuna are shared with Hatfield Township, and Christy and Eureka are shared with Bucks County and Horsham Township. Horsham, Lower Gwynedd, Upper Gwynedd, Lansdale and Hatfield all border the township.

Owners live in 89.4 percent of township homes, and turnover is low. Here is what buyers and appraisers see.

Housing measureMontgomery Township figure
Number of households9,917
Share of homes lived in by owners89.4%
Typical home value$473,400
Monthly cost for owners paying a mortgage$2,408
Monthly cost for owners with no mortgage$899
Rent, median$2,076
Household income, median$134,074

With a typical value near $473,000, a pricing gap of even a few percent is worth many thousands of dollars, so a careful price matters more here than a quick one.

Commuting buyers ask about access first:

  • U.S. 202 runs southwest to northeast through the center.
  • PA 309 runs north to south on Bethlehem Pike through Montgomery Square.
  • PA 63 follows Welsh Road along the southwestern edge, and PA 152 passes through the eastern corner on Limekiln Pike.
  • PA 463 crosses on Cowpath Road and Horsham Road.

SEPTA Suburban Bus routes 94, 96 and 132 serve Montgomery Mall, and the average commute is 29.0 minutes.

The township's fee schedule has a Use and Occupancy permit for residential property only for new construction, at $150. Other occupancy permits cover manufactured homes and non-residential space. An existing house on resale doesn't appear to need one, but call the township at (215) 393-6920 to confirm for your address. A homeowner association or your buyer's lender can add steps of their own.

Work you did on the house is a separate question. Collect your permit history before listing and gather receipts for projects that needed permits. The Codes and Permits office is at 1001 Stump Road, open weekdays 8:30 to 4:30.

The county Board of Assessment Appeals sets the values that drive your county, township and school bills. If you think yours is too high, the appeal deadline is August 1, a year before the tax year you are contesting, and exemption applications are due the same day. Hearings wrap up by October 31, and decisions go to owners and taxing districts by November 15.

The homestead exclusion lowers the taxable value of the home you live in. File by March 1 and it applies to school taxes from the following July 1. File by December 15 and it applies to municipal taxes, in municipalities that take part, from the following January 1. Selling wipes the exclusion off the parcel on its own, so you have nothing to file and the new owner starts a fresh application. If the county denies a claim, you have 40 days to appeal.

Mail can pick up a late postmark. Have the post office hand-cancel your envelope, or drop the paper off at the Norristown office.

Transfer tax on a Montgomery Township deed is 2 percent of the price. A deed claiming an exemption must carry the Department of Revenue's REV-183 Statement of Value. For deeds dated July 1, 2026 through June 30, 2027, Montgomery County's common level ratio factor is 3.36.

Pennsylvania's Seller Disclosure Law has you complete a disclosure statement and hand a signed, dated copy to the buyer before the agreement. You need not investigate, but a known defect can't be left out or misdescribed. Anything that turns inaccurate before settlement must be corrected, and a buyer has two years after settlement to bring a damages claim. Roof, basement, plumbing, heating, wiring and drainage are the usual subjects.

Unpaid taxes put a parcel at risk of the county's upset sale, which runs each September and December for properties still delinquent from two years back. Anything left unsold moves on to judicial and repository sales. Whoever wins an upset sale inherits every lien, whereas judicial sale parcels are offered free and clear.

If your house carries back taxes, you have three usual paths:

  • Pay the balance, then list as usual.
  • Sell to an owner-occupant and clear the taxes at settlement.
  • Accept an as-is cash offer from a buyer who takes on the condition.

Request a payoff figure from the tax claim bureau before choosing, because penalties and interest shift the math. A buyer paying cash can often settle the balance out of your proceeds so you never write a separate check.

Paying cash removes the lender appraisal, the loan approval and the financing contingency. Those are where financed deals most often get delayed or renegotiated. You still hand over the seller disclosure, the 2 percent transfer tax is still due as your contract directs, and the title company still pays off your mortgage and any tax balance out of the proceeds.

Before accepting an offer, confirm the name on your deed, get your loan payoff and ask the township whether any open permit needs closing out. An as-is buyer accepts the condition of the house, but unpaid taxes and liens still get settled at the table. Ask for the closing date in writing, and ask who covers recording costs.

sections.h2: Getting the house and paperwork ready
sections.html:
Gather three things first: your deed, your newest tax bill and whatever permit records the Codes and Permits office holds for the property. Then walk the house and jot down what you know about the roof, basement, plumbing, heating, wiring and drainage. That list turns into your disclosure statement, and a dated receipt for any repair backs it up.

Unpaid years? Phone the tax claim bureau. Have a mortgage? Request a payoff figure from the lender. If your deed will claim an exemption, ask for the Statement of Value form now so it is not the last thing holding up settlement.

You then pick a route. An open-market listing can reach the highest price but brings showings and a buyer's lender. A cash buyer offers a firmer closing date and fewer strangers walking through. At the closing table the title company records the deed, collects the 2 percent transfer tax and pays your loan off. What is left comes to you.

faqs.q: How much transfer tax applies to a Montgomery Township sale?
faqs.a: Two percent of the price, collected as the deed is recorded. Claiming an exemption takes a Statement of Value.

faqs.q: Does a buyer keep my homestead exclusion?
faqs.a: No. Montgomery County removes it automatically once the deed changes hands, and the new owner files a fresh application.

faqs.q: What is the last day to appeal a Montgomery County assessment?
faqs.a: August 1, one year ahead of the tax year at issue. Exemption applications share the date.

faqs.q: Is a township resale certificate needed in Montgomery Township?
faqs.a: The residential Use and Occupancy permit on the fee schedule is for new construction. Call the township at (215) 393-6920 to confirm, since your buyer's lender or an association may want other paperwork.

faqs.q: What must a Pennsylvania seller tell a buyer about the house?
faqs.a: Known material defects, listed on a property disclosure statement that is signed, dated and delivered before an agreement of transfer.
